If the previous three aspects are concealed and explained according to the most eminent state, this does not mean that empty space itself is called the Perfect Buddha.
Since the *Biefo* (Separate Buddha) is said to discuss this in isolation, it conceals the previous two aspects, just as Maudgalyāyana could not fathom the sound [of the Buddha’s voice].

If, prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three Buddhas were explained separately because they were separated by the biased and small vehicles, then upon reaching this sūtra, one distinguishes the superior from the inferior, realizing that the three are in fact one. As for others who are confused regarding the four Buddhas elucidated by our school, it is because they have discarded the previously translated sūtras and śāstras.

Just as there are four stages for attaining the Way, with the three vehicles sharing a common ground, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* for the worthy and holy ones, and the *Avataṃsaka* for the harmonious gate—these four modes of attaining the Way cannot be equated.

Because the established traces differ in their concealment of reality and covering of the fundamental, it is only by opening up the provisional and revealing the fundamental that one comes to know they are not distinct.
Furthermore, within each teaching there are five types of persons who preach the sutras; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha, śrāvakas, celestial seers, and transformed beings," while the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* adds the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings and the vessel-world (bhājanaloka), all of whom take the Buddha as their teacher;
thus, according to the four seals that establish the authority of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these are designated as the Buddha’s teaching.

Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, there is the teaching of lands and the teaching of atoms; even when Bodhisattvas receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no mention of seals (*mudrā*). As for the other three [types of] Buddha-power, they are all collectively termed "Sūtra. Therefore, that which is refuted in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as well as that which it universally encompasses fully possesses the four teachings.
If one attains the true meaning, only then will one know that the four Buddhas are identical in essence yet distinct in function.
Those who lecture on the *Avataṃsaka* all say, "This is our Buddha.

Those who read the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* do not acknowledge other scriptures; thus, it is only by reaching this present sutra that one realizes these [past] references point back to the past. Only the Buddha has fully exhausted the truth contained within these words.

Next, regarding the citation of the sutra: in the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma), the Buddha refers to "large bodies and small bodies" because he mentions an elderly bhikṣu.

In terms of the fundamental and the manifested (*honji* and *suijaku*), this first relies upon the essence and function within the fundamental; therefore, it is said that "the fundamental is one, while the manifestations are three."
Below "The Intermediate," next, the superiority and inferiority of the manifested transformations (*nirmāṇakāya*) within the traces (*jia*) are clarified.

The *parasaṃbhogakāya* (recompense body for others) all belong to the traces; however, while the terminology of "birth and extinction" mostly pertains to the manifested transformations, it is only the four Buddhas of the original ground (*mūlabhūmi*) who are all fundamentally [the Dharmakāya].

By analogy, in the provisional traces, both essence and function are trace; in the fundamental ground, both essence and function are fundamental, as explained in detail in the "Exemplary Text" (*Xuánwén*) within the section on the subtle discernment of cause and effect.
Observing that the awakening within the mind is simply wisdom, it is categorized by the "six identities.
There are editions that lack the phrase "云云" (and so forth), which may be due to textual omission.

One should first distinguish between the *zàng* and *tōng* [teachings] up to the *bié* and *yuán* [teachings], only then being able to speak of the two types of awakening—partial and perfect. Nevertheless, within the sequential [teachings], the Buddhas of both the *zàng* and *tōng* can also be subsumed; they are merely omitted here.
If one looks back from the three preceding objects and wisdoms, it refers to the Buddha as cause and condition.
The four contemplations, such as the *tathāgatagarbha*, refer to the Buddhas of the four teachings.
Looking back from the Middle Way toward emptiness and the provisional, it refers to the Buddhas of the original and the manifested.
One's own mind is precisely the Buddha of the Contemplating Mind.

Next, in the explanation of "abiding," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is utilized in its entirety; fearing that others might not understand, it first states: "the abider and the abode. If there were only body and land, they would merely constitute a world; it is through the mutual dependence of mind and phenomena that the threefold perfection (*trisiddhi*) is established.
Others maintain that while the body relies solely upon the earth, the Buddha-mind has no basis upon which it relies.
Regarding the "Endurance World" (*Sahā-lokadhātu*), the fifth fascicle of the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"For what causes and conditions is it named 'Sahā'?"
"This is because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions.
Because the subject and object are distinct, it is called the "world.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Abiding" refers to the four modes of conduct abiding in the world; in the present text, it refers to the world.
Furthermore, there are three types:
first, the celestial abode (*devasthāna*), which refers to the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in the present text, this is called the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).
The second is the Brahma-abode, which refers to the gods of the form realm; what is now called the four dhyānas is merely a difference in terminology, while in the present text it refers to humans.
The third is the Pure Abode, which refers to those from the third fruit of the path onward; what is now called the three samādhis is this same category.
The Treatise states:
"Entering the three samādhis, one immediately attains the first fruit.
Regarding the three samādhis as remedies, they serve as the proximate remedial gates for the three vidyās, as explained in detail in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
The *Śāstra* further states:

"Generosity, observance of the precepts, and a virtuous mind constitute the 'abodes of devas' (*devasthāna*); the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) constitute the 'abodes of Brahmā' (*brahmasthāna*); and the three samādhis—wherein one previously followed the fruit and here cultivates the cause—constitute the 'abodes of the noble ones' (*āryasthāna*). These abodes of the noble ones are simply the 'pure abodes' (*śuddhāvāsasthāna*)."
The treatise also mentions four abodes: those of the devas, Brahmā, the sages, and the Buddhas.
By adding the Buddha-abode, which is precisely the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* mentioned in this current text, the four abodes now encompass the entirety of the treatise’s discourse.

If categorized according to the teachings, all four teachings possess the meanings of the aforementioned four *siddhāntas*, and all four Buddhas are the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*).
However, it should simply be noted that for the first two Buddhas, one cannot say they employ the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Question:

If that is so, why does the current explanation of the Buddha’s dwelling limit itself to the three realms of desire and form, as well as the three fruits [of the śrāvaka], when neither the dweller nor the place of dwelling can be the Buddha?
Answer: First, proceeding from the general toward the specific; second, subsuming the inferior by means of the superior.
Regarding "proceeding from the general," this refers to moving from the broad to the narrow.

Regarding the phrase "following the predominant," it means that when the Buddha relies upon a royal city, he necessarily encompasses those of the desire and form realms, as well as the three fruits [of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner]. Someone objects, saying:
"Now, you explain that he dwells in a royal city; why then do you cite his dwelling among the devas and Brahmās?"
This person has never read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. This is the passage from that treatise explaining the meaning of "dwelling" (*sthiti*).

As previously stated, the treatise possesses two meanings; if one were to explain the term "dwelling" solely by means of the physical body residing in a land, then since the spirit of a great bodhisattva is without fixed location, they would have no place to dwell—how much more so for a Buddha?
Therefore, according to the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra*, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light is the Buddha’s dwelling place; how could it be the royal city?

Thus, in the subsequent section on the classification of teachings (*jiao*), Nirvana is consistently taken as the place of residence; furthermore, within that classification of teachings, all instances of Nirvana as the "dwelling dharma" refer to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the explanation that the first two Buddhas both speak of "with remainder" and "without remainder": although their skillfulness and clumsiness differ, that which is extinguished is no different; likewise, the realization of the Way within the latter two secret treasuries is also one and the same.

Regarding the judgment of "coarse" and "subtle" for the "first three Buddhas" below: although the path of realization (*darśanamārga*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-yāna*) is subtle, it is judged as coarse because it proceeds from the path of teaching (*deśanāmārga*).

As for the terms "subject" (*grāhaka*) and "object" (*grāhya*): if judged according to principle (*tattva*), it is as previously explained; if judged according to phenomena (*vastu*), it refers merely to the dependent and primary [realms] of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* land, and is therefore judged as coarse.
If one considers them according to the Middle Way (madhyamaka), although both are secret treasuries (*guhyakośa*), they are nonetheless derived from teaching (*deśanā*).
Since this present sutra is of the Perfect [Teaching], it must further be revealed and manifested; therefore, it is called the "Sublime Abode" (*miao-zhu*).

Regarding the statement in the *Ben-ji* (Prolegomena) that "the Buddha of the Tripitaka should enter nirvana," the character "should" (*ying*) is pronounced in the level tone. If one relies on the view of the "extinction of ashes" (*huai-duan*), then he "should" enter extinction; entering extinction is the "original" aspect.

It is because of compassion that he remains in the world; this "remaining in the world" is merely designated as the manifestation of traces. This Buddha’s birth as a result of retribution has no separate underlying principle. Generally speaking, Buddhas support their habitual tendencies, which is explained from the perspective of the cause: taking entry into emptuity at the sixth and seventh stages as the root, and taking the support of vows and habitual tendencies for the benefit of others as the trace. Since the fruit is identical to that of the Tripiṭaka [Śrāvaka] vehicle, it is explained from the perspective of the cause.

Regarding the statement that both the Separate and Perfect Teachings equally speak of "perfuming the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*): while there are slight differences in their scriptural authority and realization, both involve the arousal of the Four Great Vows at the appropriate time to silently perfume the dharma-nature. However, they differ in whether they clarify that the dharma-nature is identical to or distinct from [defilements]; though their wisdom and severance differ, the dharma-nature itself has no distinction.
The section beginning with "One should know" provides a general assessment of the preceding text to clarify the relationship between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku).

Since there is nothing that does not arise from compassion, and because the previous four [sections] all pertain to the manifested, it is necessary here to further speak of the abiding of the Fundamental Buddha.

From the phrase "by means of compassion" (*karuṇā*) onwards, the judgment is made that since the provisional traces (*traces*) have already been opened, how could there be a separate reality (*root*)?

Next, regarding the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the Buddha is taken to be wisdom (*jñāna*); this wisdom abides in impermanence, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Because these were previously treated directly in relation [to the four truths], the four contemplations differ.
Next, with reference to abiding in the mind, it is said: "One abides within the object by means of the dharma of non-abiding. Thus, the term "non-abiding" applies across all four teachings.

What is called "abiding" refers to coarse cognition; in reality, there is no such thing. If one is within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), this then becomes the absolute transcendence of all limitations.

Regarding "Rājagṛha" (the Royal City): according to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), this city is surrounded on all sides by lofty mountains serving as its outer wall; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty *li*. The inner city (*kumārabhavana*) is thirty *li* in circumference. The northern gate of the palace was the place where Devadatta released a drunken elephant; to the northeast is the place where Śāriputra met Aśvajit and attained the first fruit of the path. Fifteen or sixteen *li* to the northeast lies Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata*), the site where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other scriptures were preached.
The "Variegated Foot" (Pāṇḍupāda) etymology also appears in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (*Renwang jing*), and there are further alternative explanations in the treatise.
The treatise asks:
"In the case of Rājagṛha, there are also 'Abodes of Kings' in Kapilavastu and Vārāṇasī; why is this city alone given that name?"
Answer:

Some say that there was a prince of the kingdom of Magadha who had one head, two faces, and four arms; because people of the time considered him an ill omen, they tore apart his body and head and cast them into the wilderness.
There was a rākṣasī named Śarā who picked him up, gathered him together, and nurtured him with her milk.
Later, having grown to full maturity, he was able to bring many kingdoms under his rule; he then took eighty thousand kings and brought them down [to earth], as recorded in the present commentary.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* further states: "In the past, there was a king who went out hunting;

his horse bolted and he entered a treacherous wilderness where human habitation had ceased. There he lived together with a lioness and committed lewd acts. They fathered a son named Pāda-citra (Spotted Foot), who grew up to succeed the throne and lead seven hundred million followers. Due to the residual habit of eating meat, he would not eat anything except flesh; eventually, he began eating humans, and all those born of him were rākṣasas."
The remainder is largely identical to the current text.
As for the "Four Verses on Impermanence," they are simply the four verses on impermanence, as fully recorded in the seventh fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

Regarding the statement that "attaining the equality of emptiness" refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*): since this is taught in common [to both vehicles], in the Lesser Vehicle it corresponds to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), while in the Greater Vehicle it corresponds to the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) or the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*). Specifically, it refers to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which accords with the intent of the *Brahmacarya* chapter of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
If that is so, why is it that by hearing of impermanence one awakens to the Great [Vehicle]? Answer:

Having already heard of Prajñā, one hears again of non-permanence; fearing that one might be stingy regarding the kingdom, the primary and auxiliary practices are performed together, whereby great benefit is obtained.
This is categorized as belonging to the world-sphere (*loka-dhātu*) because it is distinguished by the specific karmic conditions of the spotted-footed king.

Although the thousand kings lost their small kingdoms when they drew blood from one another, their mutual awareness of the great kingdom gave rise to wholesome states; thus, it belongs to the sphere of human beings (*manuṣya-dhātu*).
The common people vacated their houses to avoid the calamity of fire; this is the "counteractive" (pratipakṣa) meaning.
That the spotted-footed bird attained the Way is the "ultimate" (paramārtha) meaning.

Regarding the note "and so forth" (*yún yún*): since the citations from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and various sutras are too numerous to be recorded in full, although they are many, they do not exceed the four *siddhāntas*. These are categorized according to the four views within the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*). However, the detailed analysis of the horizontal and vertical aspects of the lands is fully contained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, as illustrated below by the passage concerning the pure assembly of bodhisattvas and others.
Regarding "taking one as an example": this means using the Śāla tree as an analogy for the royal city.

As for the fact that the "Original" (hon) and "Trace" (jaku), as well as the "Contemplation of the Mind" (kanjin), appear later: the subsequent section clarifies the contemplation of the mind in conjunction with the text on the mountain; however, the following text remains brief and does not mention either the Original or the Trace.

If one follows the previous analogy, the latter part should state: "The Original dwells in the city of the three virtues within the King Samādhi, while the Trace resides in the royal city of the Sahā world."
Regarding the phrase "Liang Wu" and so forth, the character should be written as 睢 (*xū*). This bird resembles a hawk; as for the claim that it resembles an owl (*chī*), this is likely an error.

It is joyful yet not licentious, and sorrowful yet not wounding. The male and female each dwell apart, but when they wish to mate, they both call out together; once they have mated, they each depart. For this reason, it is used as an analogy for the imperial consorts.
The *Shijing* says:
"The *jujiu* birds call out to one another, on the islet in the river; the modest and virtuous young lady is a fitting match for the noble gentleman.
Today, the people of Jiangdong call this bird an osprey (*e*), which frequents the marshes and islands of the Yangtze.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty likely thought that the shape of Mount Sui resembled a vulture (Gṛdhra-kūṭa), and thus cited it;
this belongs to the mundane world (*loka*).
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of "mountain peaks," it is for the sake of humans, so that those who behold them may give rise to joy.
It is further said that "removing" refers to the antidote; because it can conceal evil, one must also treat evil.
Another interpretation holds that "removing" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); the abodes of the noble ones of the three vehicles constitute the ultimate truth.

Next, regarding the exposition of the five peaks and the subsequent questions and answers, these merely resolve doubts within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and differentiate the characteristics of the mountain; they are not subsumed under the four *siddhāntas*.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 31, states:
"The Buddha was at Vulture Peak and addressed the bhikṣus: 'For a long time this has been named Vulture Peak. Do you know if it has had other names?'"

It is also called Mount Guangpu (Vast and Universal), Mount Fuzhong (Carrying Heavy Loads), and Mount Xianrenku (Cavern of the Rishis). It is a place where arhats, bodhisattvas who have attained the Way, and various rishis possessing supernatural powers constantly dwell; five hundred pratyekabuddhas reside there as well.
When the Tathāgata was about to descend, he first commanded the Śuddhāvāsa devaputras to come here and issue a proclamation to purify this land.
Two years hence, the Buddha would appear in this region; having heard this, the pratyekabuddhas cremated their bodies and entered parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because there are not two Buddhas in the world, nor two kings in a kingdom; within the realm of a single Buddha, there are no two honored titles.
Likewise, the heights and depths of this mountain are also not equal.
Forty-seven states:

"The Buddha Krakucchanda traveled for four days and four nights to reach the mountain peak; Kanakamuni Buddha took three days and three nights; Kāśyapa Buddha took two days and two nights; and Śākyamuni reached the peak in a mere instant—all while traveling at the pace of a person from Rājagṛha."
"Because as time gradually reaches its end, the mountain gradually descends.

This text omits the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested; it should state that he fundamentally dwells on the mountain of Great Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues, while his manifested trace resides at Vulture Peak.
Furthermore, there is a Gṛdhrakūṭa for both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Life Span" chapter, states: "He is always on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa"; this refers to the fundamental.

Regarding the contemplation (*guan*), first one must understand the initial establishment of the object of contemplation within Rājagṛha. As for the statement "the mind-king builds the house," the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) acts as the king; since all minds that create karma necessarily possess mental factors (*caitta*), one now seeks to dissolve the "king. For the time being, the good and evil mind-kings are contrasted with the "house" of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and thus it is said that "the king builds."

The section beginning with "If one analyzes" presents four contemplations; this demonstrates that the method of contemplation differs from other sutras. It should be understood as being like the ten vehicles and ten objects (*daśayāna-daśaviṣaya*) in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan); since all subsequent sections follow this pattern, the note says "and so forth" (*yún yún*).
The subsequent two layers state, "If one contemplates," which refers to the contemplations of the latter two teachings.
One must also distinguish their respective differences in characteristics, as detailed in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (*Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*), though they cannot be fully set forth here.

When employing a mountain as the object for contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one first establishes the objective realm of the contemplation; this precisely involves contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*), as detailed in the text of the fifth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

Since it is stated within the distinct and perfect contemplations that "the mountain is itself the dharma-nature," and that the primary cause is the dharma-body while the remaining two virtues are explained according to various texts, we know that this contemplation differs from other views.

The reason for again taking the mountain as the object of contemplation is that although the mountain and the city differ, they are both *pariṇāma-niśraya* (dependent retribution). Therefore, by taking them as the object, one contemplates the *mūla-niśraya* (primary retribution).

Furthermore, the objects of all contemplations do not go beyond the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since it is convenient to categorize the present mountain and so forth according to the aggregates, various texts simply speak of "object and wisdom" (*ālambana-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "dwelling therein by oneself" and so forth: taking the meaning of both the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and this sūtra together for the sake of both self and others, one adorns oneself with the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which is precisely what is meant by "dwelling therein by oneself"; by means of this, one delivers sentient beings, which is to say, one establishes all [the Buddha's] children.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," one should likewise distinguish here the characteristics of the similarities and differences between the two contemplations; clarify the objects and the mind through skillful means and correct cultivation; and, in contrast to the preceding two, distinguish between the provisional and the real, and so on, up to the necessity of elucidating the four contemplations as well.

Next, I shall explain the character "middle" (zhōng). Since it refers to being within a mountain city, the four aspects such as causes and conditions are fully explained as in that previous commentary; here, I shall merely clarify the meaning of the character "middle."
If one wishes to explain this further, one first summarizes the manifestations to fulfill the four *siddhārtha*:
constantly delighting in the Middle Way is for the purpose of satisfying desires;
ascending to the heavens and descending from the heavens during the day is for the purpose of benefiting others.
The cessation at midnight represents the counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*);
the teaching of the Middle Way represents the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
While all teachings possess a middle way, they differ only in whether that middle way has an ontological substance or lacks one.

Regarding "root and trace": the root refers to contemplating the Middle within the perfect principle; the trace refers to demonstrating the Middle that is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
This present sutra is the Middle of revelation and clarification; if we consider it in terms of contemplation, it is "emptiness as the Middle," which encompasses both types of the Middle.
